lead: Covariance measures whether two random variables move together in a straight-line sense. It averages the product of their deviations from their own means. A positive value says high X tends to come with high Y; a negative value says high X tends to come with low Y; zero says there is no linear co-movement. Its units are units of X times units of Y, so its size is hard to read. Analysts use it in portfolio risk, quality control and signal processing, where two measurements must be judged together.
prereq: You need: joint distributions from 4.1, independence from 4.3, and expectation and variance from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Definition and the meaning of its sign

blocks.text: For random variables X and Y with means μX = E[X] and μY = E[Y], covariance is the expected product of their deviations.
Cov(X,Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E[XY] − μX μY
blocks.where: Cov(X,Y) is the covariance; E[·] is expectation; μX and μY are the means; E[XY] is the joint second moment. The second form is usually easier: find E[XY] from the joint law and subtract the product of the means.

blocks.text: Each deviation is positive when the variable is above its mean. If X and Y tend to be above their means together, the product is mostly positive and covariance is positive. If one tends to be above its mean while the other is below, the product is mostly negative and covariance is negative. The deviations cancel in the average when there is no consistent linear pattern, giving zero.

Because the deviations carry units, Cov(X,Y) carries units of X times units of Y. A covariance of 12 rupee·marks is not directly comparable with one of 0.3 metre·second. Only the sign is immediately readable. The magnitude depends on the scales of X and Y.
Covariance is symmetric: Cov(X,Y) = Cov(Y,X). Setting Y = X gives Cov(X,X) = E[(X − μX)²] = Var(X). So variance is a special covariance.

It is bilinear: for constants a, b, c and d, Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X,Y). Adding a constant does not change covariance; multiplying one variable by a scales covariance by a. Also Cov(X + Y, Z) = Cov(X,Z) + Cov(Y,Z). These rules let us expand variances without returning to the joint table.

blocks.where: The plus sign belongs to X + Y and the minus sign to X − Y. When X and Y are independent, Cov(X,Y) = 0, so the variance of a sum is the sum of variances.

blocks.text: Joint moments are E[X^i Y^j] for non-negative integers i and j. Covariance uses the moment E[XY] with i = j = 1. The joint moment generating function is M(s,t) = E[e^(sX + tY)] for real s and t near zero. Its partial derivatives at (0,0) give the joint moments, when the mgf exists. The joint mgf is developed further with the multivariate normal in 4.7.

Covariance has units, so we divide by the standard deviations. The correlation coefficient is ρ = Cov(X,Y)/(σX σY), where ρ is the correlation coefficient and σX, σY are the standard deviations of X and Y. ρ has no units and always satisfies −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1. The value +1 means Y is an increasing straight-line function of X; −1 means a decreasing straight line; 0 means no linear co-movement. Some syllabi call ρ the coefficient of linear correlation.

blocks.where: ŷ is the predicted mean of Y when X = x; μX and μY are the means; σX and σY are the standard deviations; ρ is the correlation. The slope is ρ σY/σX. The line passes through (μX, μY). The fraction of variance explained is ρ².

blocks.text: Independence implies Cov(X,Y) = 0 and hence ρ = 0, because E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]. The converse is false in general. Let X be symmetric about 0 and let Y = X². Then Cov(X,Y) = E[X³] − E[X]E[X²] = 0, yet Y is completely determined by X. So ρ = 0 says only that no straight-line trend was detected. Outside the normal case, zero correlation does not mean independence. For jointly normal variables, ρ = 0 does imply independence; see 4.7.

figure.caption: Three lines through the origin have slopes 0.9, 0 and −0.9; the sign of the slope matches the sign of the covariance.

spec.aria: Three straight lines through the origin with positive, zero and negative slopes, showing what the sign of the correlation coefficient looks like.

examples.question: Two fair dice are thrown. Let X be the number of 1s and Y the number of 2s. Find Cov(X,Y), Var(X), and the correlation coefficient ρ. Interpret the sign.
steps: Only the outcome with one 1 and one 2 gives X = 1, Y = 1 and product 1. Its probability is 2/36, because either die can be the 1. So E[XY] = 1×1×(2/36) = 1/18.
The marginal mean is μX = 2×(1/6) = 1/3. By symmetry μY = 1/3.
The variance is Var(X) = 2×(1/6)×(5/6) = 10/36 = 5/18 ≈ 0.278. By symmetry Var(Y) = 5/18.
The negative sign says outcomes with more 1s tend to have fewer 2s.
examples.answer: Cov(X,Y) = −1/18 ≈ −0.056 in count², Var(X) = Var(Y) = 5/18 ≈ 0.278, and ρ = −0.2, so 1s and 2s move in opposite directions.
examples.check:
exy = 2/36
mu = 2*(1/6)
cov = exy - mu*mu
var = 2*(1/6)*(5/6)
rho = cov/var
print(round(cov,3))
print(round(var,3))
print(round(rho,3))

traps: Concluding that ρ = 0 means independence. Outside the normal case, zero correlation rules out only a straight-line trend.
Writing Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y without the 2Cov(X,Y) term when X and Y are dependent.
Using E[XY] as covariance. Always subtract μX μY from E[XY].
Reading the size of covariance as strength. Covariance depends on units; use ρ for a scale-free measure.
For Var(X − Y), using plus instead of minus: the correct form is Var X + Var Y − 2Cov(X,Y).

quiz.q: Write the definition of Cov(X,Y) and state its units.
quiz.a: Cov(X,Y) = E[(X − μX)(Y − μY)] = E[XY] − μX μY; units are units of X times units of Y.
When X above its mean usually comes with Y below its mean, the product of deviations is usually negative, so the average is negative.

quiz.q: E[XY] = 6, μX = 2, μY = 1, Var X = 4, Var Y = 9. Find Cov(X,Y) and ρ.
X is symmetric about 0 and Y = X². Show Cov(X,Y) = 0 but X and Y are dependent.
quiz.a: E[X] = 0, so Cov = E[X·X²] − 0 = E[X³] = 0 by symmetry. Y is determined by X, so they are dependent.

quiz.q: Var X = 5, Var Y = 7, Cov(X,Y) = −2. Find Var(X + Y).
Cov(X,Y) = 5. Find Cov(−2X + 1, 3Y − 4). What happens to ρ?
quiz.a: Cov = (−2)(3)×5 = −30. ρ changes sign because the slope product is negative; its magnitude stays the same if the scales are positive.

quiz.q: State Cov(X,X) and Cov(aX + b, cY + d).
quiz.a: Cov(X,X) = Var(X); Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = ac Cov(X,Y).

beyond: Not for the exam. In finance, covariance matrices of asset returns drive portfolio variance and diversification. In machine learning, covariance describes feature spread and appears in principal component analysis. In spatial statistics, covariance functions model how nearby measurements co-vary. Search terms: covariance matrix, positive semi-definite, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis.
